newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urged by group to overhaul bank regulation.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urged by group to overhaul bank regulation.

text.p: Government regulation of financial institutions and markets is outdated and should be overhauled and scaled back, a group of financial experts recommended in a letter to President Bill Clinton on Monday.
The group urged Clinton to introduce legislation to eliminate laws enacted during the Great Depression that keep banks out of other financial service industries.

"Financial innovations, technological changes and an enhanced competitive environment have profoundly changed what financial institutions do and how they do it," the Shadow Financial Regulatory Committee, largely composed of academics at leading universities, wrote in the letter.
"Government regulation, however, has not kept pace with developments in the private sector," the group told Clinton.
Current laws, which impose different requirements and limitations on banks, insurance companies and securities firms, are "folly," the group wrote.
"A fundamental objective should be to permit financial institutions to compete across the full spectrum of financial services, without limitations by the government," it said.

To foster competition, the group urged Clinton to eliminate government subsidies and preferences in the payments system, the deposit insurance program and the Fedwire interchange -- a payment service operated by the Federal Reserve for the transfer of funds between financial instituions.

The group also recommended greater disclosure by regulators of their objectives and decision criteria. That would allow taxpayers to make a more objective evaluation of the regulators' performance, the group said.

The thrust of government regulation should be to ensure the efficiency and stability of the payments system, not to maintain the solvency of individual financial institutions or to protect uninsured depositors, non-deposit creditors or the stockholders of individual institutions, the group said.
